small_guidance:
- The runtime is dominated by ConvTranspose2d (the post-conv reduction kernel is trivially small relative to a 16×128×514×514 output). Tuning BLOCK_HW/num_warps on the partial-sum kernel will not move the needle; only replacing/fusing the conv will.
- If staying in this structure, try a single-pass reduction kernel (one program per (N, C) reducing all HW in registers with a long inner loop) to drop the intermediate `partial` tensor — but expected gain is <1%.
large_guidance:
- Replace `nn.ConvTranspose2d` with a custom Triton scatter-add kernel: for each (N, IC, H, W) input tile, compute the outer product with the (IC, OC, kh, kw) weight and scatter-add into the (N, OC, H+kh-1, W+kw-1) output. Tile over (N, OC_block, output spatial block); kernel_size=3 with stride=1 means each input contributes to a 3×3 neighborhood — handle padding/edges with masks.
- Fuse the conv epilogue with the global-mean reduction: instead of materializing the (N, 128, 514, 514) output, have each program accumulate per-(N, OC) partial sums into a small (N, OC, num_tiles) buffer, then a tiny second kernel does mean + bias + logsumexp + sum×10. This avoids a ~17 GB write/read of the conv output, which is the actual bottleneck.
- Alternative: implement conv-transpose as an im2col-style gather GEMM over (N·H_out·W_out, OC) × (IC·kh·kw, OC)^T with channels-last layout; autotune BLOCK_M/N/K = {64,128} × {64,128} × {32,64}, num_warps∈{4,8}, num_stages∈{2,3}. Fuse the global mean into the GEMM epilogue by reducing across the M (spatial) dimension before writeback.
